blocks.en: Hello, young explorers, and welcome back to Michael's Morning Listening!
Today we visit two wonders of the desert.
First, a ski resort in the middle of hot sand, with real snow!
Then, a tiny fish that swims in water almost too hot to touch.
Ready?
Let's go!
In Dubai, a city in the middle of the desert, there is a ski resort inside a huge shopping mall.
Outside, the sun bakes the sand.
Inside, it is winter all year round!
The temperature stays around minus two degrees, and real snow covers the slopes.
Here are some amazing statistics: there are five slopes, and the longest run is four hundred metres long.
Every night, snow machines make fresh snow, and it accumulates into a soft white mountain.
Thick walls and double doors make sure the cold air does not leak out.
Meanwhile, visitors put on warm jackets and boots — the resort lends them all for free!
Families come here to ski, snowboard, and build snowmen.
Children race down on sleds, and friends have snowball fights.
If you stay late, the snow park glows with coloured lights.
And here is the biggest surprise: visitors also get the chance to meet real penguins!
King penguins and gentoo penguins waddle around their icy home, and they seem to approve of the cold.
Skiing together in the desert is a wonderful way for families to bond.
Now we travel to Death Valley in America, one of the hottest places on Earth.
Among the rocks and sand, there are small pools of warm spring water.
And in that water lives a tiny hero: the desert pupfish.
It is only about four centimetres long — smaller than your thumb!
This little fish is a champion of survival.
In summer, its pool can heat up to forty-seven degrees — almost too hot to touch!
In winter, the same water can drop to zero.
And the water is four times saltier than the ocean.
Most fish would not last a day here.
The males turn bright blue in the mating season.
How does it do it?
Special cells in its gills and kidneys work like tiny filters, keeping the salt balance just right.
When the water gets low in oxygen, the pupfish rises to the surface, where the air meets the water.
Rangers check the health of the springs every week, because these fish live nowhere else on Earth.
One more pupfish lives in a single desert-cave pool, where the water stays around thirty-four degrees all year.
Only a few hundred are left.
Here's today's idiom: 'under the weather.' When you feel under the weather, you feel a little sick — not seriously ill, just not quite yourself!

Here's an example: 'After skiing all day in the cold, Tom felt under the weather, so he stayed home with hot soup and a good book.' So next time your nose is runny or your head feels heavy, you can say: 'I'm feeling a bit under the weather today.'
Let's think about our stories: a ski resort in the desert, and a tiny fish in hot water.
First: if you could build something impossible in the desert — a snow mountain, an ice palace, anything — what would you build, and why?
Second: the pupfish survives the hottest water by changing how its body works.
What helps you feel better on a very hot day?
Talk about it with your family!
That's all for today, young explorers.
Stay curious, stay brave — and if you ever feel under the weather, rest well and come back stronger!
See you tomorrow!
